title: Solitude in the crowd
hook: Naqshbandi Sufis keep a silent remembrance going while living ordinary lives

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Ghazali's crisis: a doubt that argument couldn't cure, and a way through by tasting. Your line was lost, then found. Where did you step away, and did anything come clear? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.

A market at noon. Carts, voices, prices called across the stalls, someone haggling over a roll of cloth. In the middle of it a merchant is doing ordinary business: weighing, counting, smiling at a regular customer. And inside, silently, without a word on his lips, he is remembering God. Nobody around him can tell. That scene is the picture behind a short Persian phrase that Naqshbandi Sufis keep close: khalwat dar anjuman. Solitude in the crowd. Today is about how a person can be alone like that, in the middle of everyone.
screen: `A MARKET AT NOON.` → `SILENT, INSIDE.` → `KHALWAT DAR ANJUMAN.`

segments.voice: The Naqshbandi order is one of the Sufi paths, named for Baha al-Din Naqshband. Its teachers kept a handful of short Persian phrases as signposts for the way, and solitude in the crowd is one of them. It means: outwardly with people, inwardly with God. A saying handed down in the order puts it even more simply: the hand at work, the heart with the Friend. The Naqshbandi way puts its weight on silent remembrance, dhikr of the heart, rather than remembrance said aloud. So a Naqshbandi can trade, cook, raise children, ride a crowded train, and keep the remembrance running underneath, unheard. Beside this phrase the order keeps others just as short. Awareness in the breath. Watch your step, eyes on where your feet are going. A journey inside your own homeland. Together they describe a path that doesn't need a cave. The Qur'an gives a picture of it, in Pickthall's translation: "Men whom neither merchandise nor sale beguileth from remembrance of Allah." Look closely at that verse. The merchandise is still there. So is the sale. The market doesn't vanish. What changes is whether it pulls the heart away. There's a tension here worth naming. Other Sufis go off into retreat, away from everyone, and tomorrow is about that. The Naqshbandi phrase doesn't throw retreat out. It carries it into the street. The solitude is real. It just doesn't need an empty room.
screen: `OUTWARDLY WITH PEOPLE, INWARDLY WITH GOD.` · `THE HAND AT WORK, THE HEART WITH THE FRIEND.` · `REMEMBRANCE IN SILENCE.` · `RETREAT CARRIED INTO THE STREET.` · then, large: `NEITHER MERCHANDISE NOR SALE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice silently in a crowd, starting wherever you are. Settle, and breathe. Listen for the sounds of other people: voices, traffic, a door down the hall, a television somewhere. Don't shut them out. Let them be the market around you. Then, underneath, keep one quiet thing going. If you pray, a word of remembrance, silent, carried on the breath. If you don't, simply the breath itself, noticed, in and out. The noise goes on. The quiet thing keeps running under it. The bell holds the time.
Solitude in the crowd. In Persian, khalwat dar anjuman: a Naqshbandi Sufi phrase for silent remembrance kept up in the middle of ordinary life. Today's word.

Your line: alone in the crowd. Today, the next time you're among people, in a line, on a bus, at a busy table, keep one silent thing running underneath for a minute. Nobody needs to know. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Naqshbandi Sufis are taught a silent remembrance of the heart, kept up through work and family life, guided by short Persian principles such as solitude in the crowd and awareness in the breath.

notes: Confirm Pickthall wording of 24:37: 'Men whom neither merchandise nor sale beguileth from remembrance of Allah'.

The Naqshbandi principles are often listed as a set (traditionally attributed in part to Abd al-Khaliq Ghujduvani, with additions by Baha al-Din Naqshband); the script gives no count and no attribution beyond 'its teachers'. Confirm.
'The hand at work, the heart with the Friend' (dast ba kar, dil ba yar) is described as 'a saying handed down in the order'; it is commonly attributed to Baha al-Din Naqshband. Confirm.
'The Naqshbandi way puts its weight on silent remembrance' (dhikr khafi): confirm phrasing; some Naqshbandi branches also practice vocal dhikr.
The market scene in the hook is an illustration, not a sourced story.
